09 Slide deck outline

BMED Chapter 14 (communicating your design). One slide per row: suggested title, the point to make, the figure to show, and the numbers to quote. All figures are in docs/figures/; all numbers come from evaluation/results/.

Suggested length: 18 slides, about 15–18 minutes. Slides marked ★ carry the argument; the rest can be trimmed.

#Slide titleKey message (say this)VisualNumbers to quote
1Hemodynamic decision support: choosing how to deploy a physics-informed modelOne model, five ideas, three concepts, one choice backed by evidenceui02_concept_a.png (cropped banner + forecast)–
2 ★The problemMonitors alarm after hypotension; most alarms are noiseShort text + one citation eachMAP < 55 linked to AKI / myocardial injury (Walsh 2013); 72–99% alarms non-actionable (Sendelbach & Funk 2013)
3Project statementTechnology push from Version 5; the MadLib (doc 01 §3)MadLib text, needs and barriers highlighted–
4StakeholdersNurses carry the alarm burden; physicians decide; FDA gatesPower and influence table (doc 01 §5)–
5 ★Specifications15 measurable design inputs; must-meet vs trade-offTable 4.3-style excerpt (doc 02 §2): SPEC-01, 02, 04, 05, 07, 11, 15Ideal / marginal values
6BenchmarkingHPI predicts minutes ahead; we predict 15 s; persistence is a hard baselineBenchmark table (doc 02 §4)HPI 0.88 / 0.87; persistence 2.6 mmHg real
7 ★From 5 briefs to 3 concepts1 + 2 + 3 share user, moment and data → merge; 4 and 5 differ in setting / timefig01_concept_confluence.png–
8The prototype: one app, three conceptsShared engine = fair comparisonfig02_architecture.png + ui01_overview.pngCPU p95 175 ms
9Concept A in actionExplained alerts, forecast band, treatment responseui04_concept_a_intervention.pngVasopressor: MAP +30 mmHg, "improving"
10 ★Storyboard: same patient, A vs BA escalates WATCH → DETERIORATING → CRITICAL; B stays STABLE at ~74 while true MAP is 49fig11_example_case.pngA: DETERIORATING at 00:59 at MAP 65.9, 1 s before the threshold alarm
11 ★Verification: who meets the specifications?Only A passes every must-meet specificationfig03_spec_scorecard.pngA real: sensitivity 0.96, specificity 0.87, AUROC 0.96, MAE 4.7 mmHg; B real AUROC 0.59
12 ★The hazard we found (H-09)Version 5 discarded real pressure in deep shock, so less information meant more reassurance; layered controls fixed itfig07_hazard_h09_layers.pngUnder-alert 53% → 0.18%; unsafe de-escalations 41 → 0
13Signal-quality gateVersion 5 forecast "normal" on 40% PPG drop-out; RC-07 fixed itfig08_quality_gate.png24% → 100% handled; genuine shock ABP kept 52% → 95%
14Risk management6 unacceptable risks → 1 (Concept B's false reassurance)fig12_fmea_risk_chart.png13 risks; R-04 stays unacceptable
15 ★Concept selectionGate → matrix → DSM with rotated datum → House of Quality → sensitivityfig04_decision_matrix.png + fig05_dsm_rotated_datum.pngA 3.95 (HoQ 4.15), C 3.60, B 2.00, current practice 3.70
16 ★Is the decision robust? (be honest)C wins under equal weights and 66% of random weightings, but cannot detect in real time (gate); A wins whenever detection carries ≥ 9.5% weightfig06_weight_sensitivity.pngBreak-even 9.5% vs our 20%
17 ★Decision and next iterationSelect A + C's report; defer B. Next: longer horizon, quieter WATCH, R/C-preserving training, usability studySummary bulletsPersistence beats the model on average (2.1 vs 4.3 mmHg) but not during change (8.5 vs 10.0)
18Validation plan and limitationsVerified, not yet validated; plan V2–V6Table from doc 07 §830 real cases, single centre

Lines for the selection slide (slide 15–17)

"We chose Concept A because it is the only concept that meets every must-meet specification. It discriminates hypotension well on unseen real patients (AUROC 0.96, 4.7 mmHg error), it is fail-safe by design (it can never be less safe than the existing monitor), and it is the only concept that tells clinicians whether their treatment is working. Concept B looked attractive for lower-resource settings, but it missed every critical-hypotension period in testing; that risk is unacceptable under ISO 14971. Concept C scores well on documentation and low risk, so we kept its report as a module of A rather than as a separate product. A's honest weakness is lead time: at a 15-second horizon it is only seconds ahead of a threshold alarm, so extending the horizon is our next design iteration."

Questions to prepare for

Likely questionAnswer and evidence
"Why not just use the current MAP?"At 15 s, persistence is more accurate on average (2.1 vs 4.3 mmHg). The model's value is during change (8.5 vs 10.0) and in discrimination plus explanation. Hence the horizon recommendation (doc 07 §4)
"Your weights decided the outcome."The gate decides before the weights. Under single pessimistic re-scorings A still wins; C wins only if detection gets < 9.5% weight (doc 04 §8)
"Is this better than HPI?"It is not comparable yet: HPI forecasts 5–15 min ahead. Our contribution is the fail-safe alert layer and treatment-response view (doc 02 §4)
"Why does A alarm so much?"WATCH-level burden is 12.6/h on real data vs 5.5 for the monitor; planned fix is WATCH as a non-alarming information signal (FMEA R-05)
"Is the R/C output trustworthy?"No, not after fine-tuning (r = 0.54 / 0.03); shown as trends only, not used for alerts (doc 07 §6)
"Were the test patients in training?"No. Held-out test splits only; calibration on validation splits only (doc 07 §1)
